basic_identification.name: Human-machine co-creation
basic_identification.originator: Sougwen Chung (DOUG/Drawing Operations Unit, SCILICET studio), Memo Akten (computational artist, PhD Goldsmiths), Patrick Tresset (drawing robots), Ian Cheng (simulations), Holly Herndon & Mat Dryhurst (Holly+, Spawning), Hito Steyerl (critical-theoretical), Botto (decentralized autonomous artist)
basic_identification.geography: Global. Key nodes: New York (Chung), London/Istanbul (Akten), Berlin (Herndon/Dryhurst, Steyerl), distributed online communities (Botto DAO)

core_ideas.core_claim: Distinct from AI-as-tool (where the human directs and the machine executes), human-machine co-creation positions AI systems as collaborative agents with their own responsiveness, unpredictability, and emergent behavior. The creative act arises from a feedback loop between human and machine, where both parties shape the output. As Sougwen Chung articulates: the robots 'don't follow commands; they respond, improvise, and evolve alongside the artist. It's a dialogue, not a dictation.'
core_ideas.medium_specificity: Digitally native in its dependency on machine learning, computer vision, robotics, and biofeedback systems. The practice could not exist without computational systems capable of learning, responding, and generating in real time. The medium specificity lies in the feedback loop itself — the real-time exchange between human gesture/intention and machine response/generation that constitutes a new form of creative agency.
core_ideas.relation_to_attention_economy: Largely resistant to attention economy logic. The practice is process-oriented, research-intensive, and slow. Chung's DOUG project spans a decade of iterative development. Akten's work is grounded in PhD research and philosophical inquiry. The work circulates through museums, galleries, and academic channels rather than platform metrics. However, high-profile visibility (Chung at Davos 2025, TIME100 AI list) generates attention-economy effects as a byproduct.
core_ideas.relation_to_intention: Strongly intention-native. The practice serves declared structural needs: understanding human-machine relations, developing new models of creative agency, questioning automation narratives, and building alternative frameworks for AI in culture. It is driven by research questions, not engagement metrics. Chung's progression through six DOUG generations over a decade exemplifies long-term intentional development.

market_economics.revenue_model: Gallery sales of physical co-created works (paintings, sculptures), institutional commissions, museum exhibitions, speaking fees (Davos, TED), academic positions, grants, venture funding for technology ventures (Herndon/Dryhurst's Spawning). Chung founded SCILICET studio. Some practitioners have gallery representation. Botto operates through a DAO with token-based economics and auction sales.
market_economics.market_position: Primary art market (gallery sales of co-created works), institutional commissions, research/academic positions. Not primarily a secondary market practice. Infrastructure position through tool development (Spawning, Holly+). Bridges art market and technology sector.
market_economics.price_range: Gallery works: $10,000-$500,000+ for established practitioners (Chung, Akten). Botto DAO works: auction prices from $50,000-$800,000+. Emerging practitioners: $2,000-$20,000. The price reflects the artist's reputation and the conceptual significance of the human-machine collaboration process. [uncertain]
market_economics.volume_trend_2024_2026: Growing steadily. The discourse around AI creativity has made human-machine co-creation a central topic in contemporary art. Chung's visibility at Davos 2025, V&A performances, and TIME100 recognition indicate increasing institutional interest. The practice benefits from broader AI discourse without being captured by AI art market hype. Growth is organic and reputation-driven, not speculative.
market_economics.collector_demographics: Institutional collectors (museums: Buffalo AKG, V&A), technology industry collectors interested in AI art, contemporary art collectors drawn to conceptual innovation, research institutions. Botto attracts crypto-native collectors through its DAO model. The audience is educated, technologically literate, and interested in the philosophical dimensions of AI. [uncertain]
market_economics.sustainability: Moderate to high. The practice's sustainability rests on multiple pillars: gallery sales for established artists, institutional commissions, academic positions, speaking engagements, and technology ventures. It does not depend on speculative markets. The durability of the central question (what is creative agency when machines can create?) ensures continued relevance. Risk: if AI co-creation becomes commonplace, the practice may lose its distinctive position.

practice_aesthetics.toolchain: Custom robotic systems (Chung's DOUG arms), machine learning frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch), computer vision (OpenCV, depth cameras), biofeedback sensors (EEG headsets, heart rate monitors, full-body tracking), custom neural networks trained on artist data, GANs, diffusion models, reinforcement learning, robotic arms (industrial and custom), spatial computing tools. Akten uses real-time interactive systems with continuous feedback. Herndon uses custom voice synthesis models.
practice_aesthetics.relation_to_AI: AI is the co-creative partner, not a tool. This is the defining distinction: AI systems have agency, unpredictability, and emergent behavior within the creative process. Chung trains neural networks on her own drawing data, creating systems that produce 'similar but not identical' outputs — the errors becoming generative. Akten frames the relationship as conductor-to-orchestra or art director-to-designer. Herndon trained a model on her own voice, creating a 'digital twin' that extends her creative capacity.
practice_aesthetics.liveness: High liveness. Most works involve real-time performance or real-time interaction between human and machine. Chung's DOUG performances are live. Akten's installations are interactive with real-time feedback loops. The outputs (paintings, recordings) are artifacts of live processes. The liveness is essential — the work is the process of co-creation, not just the output.
practice_aesthetics.aesthetic_vocabulary: Developing rapidly. Key terms: co-creation, collaborative agency, feedback loop, error-as-generative, biomimetic, biofeedback, digital puppetry, human-in-the-loop, centaur model, symbiosis, entanglement, non-human agency. Chung introduced 'poeticize error' and 'ecologies of becoming-with.' Akten contributed 'action-perception loops' and the art director/conductor analogies. The vocabulary draws from robotics, cognitive science, and posthumanist philosophy. Academic discourse (NIME, CHI conferences, Taylor & Francis publications) provides formal critical vocabulary. Mainstream art criticism is still developing adequate terms.
practice_aesthetics.tendency_axis_position: Tends toward openness (research-oriented, knowledge-sharing), commons (academic publications, some open-source tools), infrastructure (building new frameworks for understanding AI creativity), and individual-to-collective (individual studio practice but contributing to collective understanding). The practice sits on the infrastructure and openness ends of the axes, though commercial gallery practice introduces enclosure elements.

infrastructure_governance.openness: Mixed. Academic research is published openly. Akten's conceptual frameworks are shared through papers and talks. Herndon/Dryhurst's Spawning is an open platform. But studio-specific systems (Chung's DOUG, custom neural networks) are proprietary as creative infrastructure. The practice contributes to shared knowledge (concepts, frameworks, vocabulary) more than shared technical tools.
infrastructure_governance.governance_model: Individual studio practice (Chung's SCILICET, Akten's solo practice) with academic affiliation. Botto operates as a DAO with token-holder governance. No field-level governance structure. Individual artists make autonomous decisions about their practice, collaboration terms, and technology sharing.
infrastructure_governance.data_sovereignty: Complex. Artists train AI on their own data (Chung's drawings, Herndon's voice), maintaining sovereignty over training data. But the resulting models raise questions: who owns the outputs of a system trained on one artist's data? Herndon's Holly+ explicitly addresses this through licensing. Chung's SCILICET studio controls DOUG's outputs. The practice is more thoughtful about data sovereignty than most AI art practices.
infrastructure_governance.interoperability: Low. Each practitioner's system is custom-built. DOUG does not interoperate with Holly+. No standard protocol for human-machine co-creation. The practice produces concepts that transfer (feedback loops, error-as-generative) but not technical infrastructure. Academic publications serve as a conceptual interoperability layer.
infrastructure_governance.preservation_strategy: Mixed. Physical co-created works (paintings, sculptures) are preserved through standard art conservation. Performance documentation exists as video. The systems themselves (custom robots, trained models) face preservation challenges: hardware degrades, software dependencies change, model weights may become incompatible. Institutional acquisitions provide some preservation guarantee for outputs but rarely for the systems. The process is harder to preserve than the product.
infrastructure_governance.consent_architecture: Thoughtful but informal. Artists consent to train AI on their own data (self-consent). Herndon's Holly+ addresses voice consent through explicit licensing. Chung's biofeedback works raise questions about body data consent in performance contexts. Spawning's 'Have I Been Trained?' tool is the most significant consent infrastructure contribution. The practice engages with consent questions conceptually but lacks formalized machine-readable consent protocols.

field_position.relation_to_traditional_art_world: Integrated but distinctive. Major museum exhibitions (V&A, ACMI Melbourne), gallery representation (some practitioners), academic positions, prestigious recognition (TIME100 AI, Ars Electronica awards). The work is legible to the art world as contemporary art practice while pushing its boundaries. The human element (Chung painting alongside robots, Akten performing) provides continuity with art-world expectations of authorship.
field_position.what_it_enables: A third position beyond AI-as-tool and AI-as-threat: AI-as-collaborator. New forms of creative expression through human-machine feedback loops. Practical models for how artists can engage with AI without being replaced by it. Philosophical frameworks for understanding non-human creative agency. A humanistic counter-narrative to automation anxiety.
field_position.what_it_lacks: Scalability — the practice requires deep technical expertise and custom systems. Critical mass of practitioners — still a small field. Standardized tools or platforms that would lower barriers to entry. Economic models accessible to emerging artists (custom robotics is expensive). A clear boundary between co-creation and sophisticated tool use (when does using Midjourney become co-creation?). Systematic documentation of processes and methodologies that could be taught and transmitted.
field_position.who_is_excluded: Artists without technical expertise (programming, robotics, ML). Those without access to expensive hardware (robotic arms, sensors, GPUs). Artists outside institutional/academic networks that provide resources. Practitioners from regions without AI research infrastructure. The practice requires significant capital investment in technology that most artists cannot afford. The philosophical framing may exclude practitioners who engage with AI through commercial tools rather than custom systems. [uncertain]
field_position.frontier_signal: Frontier practice, rapidly gaining institutional recognition. The central question (what is collaborative creative agency between humans and machines?) is becoming more urgent as AI capabilities expand. The practice is transitioning from niche experimentation to recognized art-world category. Chung's Davos 2025 appearance and TIME100 listing signal mainstream visibility. The frontier extends into biosensor-driven creation, multi-agent systems, and collective human-machine co-creation.

attention_intention.discovery_mechanism: Museum exhibitions, art publications (Art Newspaper, MIT Technology Review, Dazed, designboom), academic conferences (NIME, CHI, ISEA), institutional programming (V&A, ACMI, WEF), social media documentation (secondary), word of mouth within AI art communities. Discovery is curated and institutional rather than algorithm-driven.
attention_intention.attention_dependency: Low. The practice would survive platform disappearance. Discovery happens through institutional channels, academic networks, and personal reputation. Social media amplifies but is not essential. The work's value lies in the process and conceptual framework, not in viral moments. Chung's decade-long DOUG project demonstrates attention-independence.
attention_intention.intention_alignment: Strongly intention-native. Serves the field's need for frameworks to understand human-machine creative relations. Contributes to critical discourse on AI and creativity. Develops alternative narratives to automation replacement. The practice is driven by research questions and artistic inquiry, not engagement metrics.
attention_intention.commons_contribution: Moderate to high. Academic publications share conceptual frameworks openly. Akten's theoretical writings are freely available. Herndon/Dryhurst's Spawning is public infrastructure. Chung's talks and interviews disseminate ideas. The practice contributes significantly to shared vocabulary and conceptual commons, less to shared technical tools.

provenance_temporality.provenance_type: Both ownership and meaning provenance. Physical co-created works have standard art market ownership provenance. But the practice also tracks meaning provenance: which generation of DOUG was used, what training data informed the model, how the human-machine relationship evolved. Chung's generational framework (DOUG 1-6) is itself a provenance system for tracing the evolution of a human-machine relationship.
provenance_temporality.temporal_logic: Deep-historical and evolutionary. Chung's decade-long DOUG project tracks the evolution of a human-machine relationship over time. Akten's career-long investigation of feedback loops builds cumulatively. The practice values long-term development over trend-following. The temporal logic is more geological than seasonal.
provenance_temporality.absence_handling: Actively addresses absences. The practice identifies what is missing: nuanced frameworks for AI creativity (beyond tool vs. threat), models of non-human agency, humanistic approaches to automation. Chung's work addresses the absence of embodiment in AI discourse. Akten addresses the absence of meaningful human control in generative AI. The practice is fundamentally oriented toward filling conceptual gaps.

coherence.coherence_vs_consensus: Coherence. Practitioners share core commitments (AI as collaborator, importance of feedback loops, value of unpredictability) while pursuing radically different approaches. Chung works with physical robots, Akten with real-time visual systems, Herndon with voice synthesis, Botto with autonomous generation + DAO curation. The coherence is at the level of questions asked, not methods used.
coherence.contestability: High. The fundamental question — does a machine truly 'co-create' or is this anthropomorphization? — is actively contested in philosophy, cognitive science, and art criticism. Akten explicitly resists the 'AI art' label, preferring 'computational art.' The boundary between co-creation and tool use is constantly debated. Academic peer review provides formal contestation mechanisms.
coherence.forkability: Conceptually high, technically low. The idea of human-machine co-creation can be adapted by anyone. But replicating specific systems (DOUG, Holly+) requires deep technical expertise. The conceptual framework is infinitely forkable; the technical implementation is not. This is both a strength (ideas spread freely) and a limitation (practice remains elite).

adai_comparison.what_adai_should_adopt: The feedback loop model as a design pattern for human-AI interaction in A(DAI). The 'poeticize error' principle — treating system imperfections as generative rather than failures to be eliminated. The generational development model (DOUG 1-6) as a template for evolving human-machine relationships over time. Akten's art director/conductor analogy for meaningful human control over AI systems. The insistence on embodiment and physicality as a corrective to purely screen-based AI interaction.
adai_comparison.what_adai_should_refuse: The individual-genius model that concentrates creative authority in single artists with custom systems. The high technical barriers that exclude most practitioners. The art-world dependency for validation and economic sustainability. The tendency to anthropomorphize machine behavior rather than developing new categories for non-human agency. The lack of standardized, shareable tools that could democratize the practice.
adai_comparison.structural_tension: Human-machine co-creation develops deep, individual human-AI relationships; A(DAI) aims for collective intelligence infrastructure. The practice is studio-centric; A(DAI) is commons-centric. The tension is productive: A(DAI) needs the conceptual depth of co-creation research while scaling its insights from individual studios to collective infrastructure. How do you maintain the feedback loop's intimacy at the scale of a field-wide intelligence system?

regulatory_legal.regulatory_exposure: Moderate and growing. AI-generated outputs face copyright uncertainty (US Copyright Office ruling that purely AI-generated works are not copyrightable). Co-created works with clear human involvement likely retain copyright protection, but the boundary is legally untested. EU AI Act may require transparency about AI involvement in creative works. Biofeedback data (EEG, body tracking) faces health data regulations. Herndon's Holly+ faces voice rights and deepfake regulations.
regulatory_legal.ip_model: Mixed. Co-created physical works follow standard art market IP (artist retains copyright, galleries handle reproduction rights). AI model weights and training data raise unresolved IP questions. Herndon's Holly+ uses explicit licensing for voice model use. Botto's DAO model creates novel IP ownership structures (community-owned autonomous artist). No established legal framework for co-created human-machine IP.
regulatory_legal.opt_in_vs_opt_out: Opt-in for most elements. Artists voluntarily train AI on their own data (self-consent). Spawning's platform enables opt-in/opt-out for training data inclusion. Biofeedback participation is voluntary. The practice generally defaults to opt-in consent, partly because the practitioners are themselves the primary data subjects.

ecosystem.platform_dependency: Low to moderate. The practice does not depend on any single platform, blockchain, or cloud service. Some dependency on ML frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch) and hardware suppliers (robotic arm manufacturers). Botto depends on Ethereum blockchain. Gallery relationships provide economic stability but are not a single point of failure. The practice is relatively platform-resilient.
ecosystem.network_effects: Moderate. More practitioners develop more concepts, tools, and visibility, attracting more interest. Academic networks create citation and collaboration effects. But the practice does not require critical mass — a single artist with a custom system can produce significant work. Network effects are intellectual (shared discourse) rather than platform-based.
ecosystem.post_crash_trajectory: Largely unaffected by the 2022-2023 crypto/NFT crash. The practice never depended on speculative markets (with the partial exception of Botto's DAO model). Growth continues through institutional recognition, museum exhibitions, and the broader cultural conversation about AI. Chung's Davos 2025 appearance and V&A performances indicate upward trajectory. The practice benefits from AI discourse expansion without being captured by AI art market dynamics.
